title: Slow breath, deeper
hookLine: breathing at about six breaths a minute, with heart-rate biofeedback, has research support for stress and mood (Lehrer)

lines: THE HEART SPEEDS UP, THEN EASES OFF.
A WEEK OF THE HONEST PART.
WHEN THE BREATH SLOWS TO MEET IT.
cards: Your heart doesn't keep a perfectly even beat, and that's good news. Breathe in, and it speeds up a little. Breathe out, and it eases off.
Two fingers on the inside of the wrist can sometimes catch it happening. This week has asked what holds up: an open placebo, prayer in a lab, showing up, a tiny ritual, singing together, fasting.
It ends with something nobody has to believe in at all: that small rise and fall of the heart, and what happens when the breath slows down to meet it.

teach.b: First, the wave. That speeding up and easing off with each breath is normal. Researchers call the change from beat to beat heart rate variability.
Second, the resonance. The psychologist Paul Lehrer and his colleagues worked with a simple idea.

When people slow their breathing to around six breaths a minute, the heart's rise and fall lines up with the breath, and the waves grow larger, like pushing a child on a swing at just the right moment in each arc: small pushes, big swing.

They called that pace the resonance frequency, and found it differs a little from person to person. Third, the evidence. With a screen showing their heart rhythm, people can learn to breathe right at that pace.
This is heart rate variability biofeedback. Reviews of the studies have found it helps some people with stress, anxiety and low mood.
It isn't a cure, and it isn't for everything, but it's one of the breath practices with real research behind it. Fourth, the old company.
Breath has been a teacher on several paths: yoga's pranayama, Buddhist mindfulness of breathing, Orthodox Christians who join the Jesus Prayer to the breath.

teach.h: BIOFEEDBACK: REAL SUPPORT, NOT A CURE.
teach.b: None of them needed a heart monitor.

teach.h: AN OLD TEACHER, A NEW REASON.
teach.b: What the lab adds is a pace you can count, and a reason it might work.
When breath and heartbeat move together, something in the body rings like a struck bell.

how: Therapists who use heart rate variability biofeedback coach people to breathe slowly, often near six breaths a minute, while a screen shows their heart rhythm; similar slow breathing appears in yoga, Buddhist and Christian contemplative practice.

games.q: you push a child on a swing. when do small pushes make the biggest swing?
o: at just the right moment in each arc.
games.why: timing is everything. Lehrer's resonance idea is the same: at the right breathing pace, breath and heart rhythm line up and the waves grow.

practice: Breathe at about six a minute, roughly ten seconds for each whole breath: in gently through the nose for a slow count of four, out a little longer for a slow count of six.
Don't force it or fill up hard, and if you feel lightheaded, let the breath go back to normal for a while. When the rhythm holds itself, let the count fade.

wordCard.voice: Slow breath. Around six breaths a minute, breath and heart rhythm line up, and biofeedback built on that has research support for stress and mood. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, from the yoga tradition: a name for breath practice.

carryVoice: Your line: resonant. In for four, out for six is there whenever stress rises. Breathe easy.
